title: Halving: O(log n) and O(n log n)
summary: Loops that halve their work each time, and why they stay fast at any size.

steps.title: Halving is shockingly fast
body: Some loops do not walk the data one item at a time: they **cut it in half** each pass. How many halvings until one item is left?
That number is the **logarithm base 2** of `n`, written `log n`. Watch `n` shrink below: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Five steps.
A thousand times more data costs only **10 more steps**. That is `O(log n)`.

steps.prompt: Integer division rounds down. What does this print?
steps.explain: 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1: nine halvings. log₂ 1000 is about 9.97, rounded down by integer division.
hints: Write out the values: 1000, 500, 250, ... and count the arrows.

steps.prompt: Binary search halves a sorted list on every step. About how many steps does it need for **one million** items?
steps.explain: 2²⁰ is 1,048,576, so twenty halvings take a million down to one.

steps.title: O(n log n): a halving loop, n times
body: Put a halving loop **inside** a normal loop and you get `n × log n`. Good sorting algorithms (merge sort, the one .NET uses) land here.
With `n = 8` the inner loop runs 3 times (8 → 4 → 2 → 1) for each of the 8 outer passes: 24 steps.
`n log n` is a little worse than `n` and enormously better than `n²`: for a million items it is about 20 million steps against a trillion.

steps.prompt: This loop **doubles** instead of halving. What does it print?
steps.explain: `i` takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64: seven of them before reaching 128. Doubling up to `n` is also `O(log n)`.

steps.prompt: Arrange from **slowest-growing** (best for big data) at the top to **fastest-growing** at the bottom.
steps.explain: `O(2ⁿ)` doubles with every single extra item: 60 items is already more steps than any computer can do.

items: `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` then `for (j = 0; j < n; j++)` (one after the other)
`for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 1; j < n; j *= 2)`
steps.explain: Stepping by 2 halves the count but it is still a straight line: `n / 2` is `O(n)`. Multiplying or dividing the loop variable is what gives `log n`.

steps.title: Count the halvings
prompt: - `int Log2Floor(int n)`: how many times you can halve `n` (integer division) before it reaches 1. `Log2Floor(1)` is 0, `Log2Floor(32)` is 5, `Log2Floor(1000)` is 9.
- `int DigitCount(int n)`: how many decimal digits `n` has, for `n >= 0`. `DigitCount(0)` is 1, `DigitCount(4096)` is 4. (This is a base-10 logarithm in disguise: divide by 10.)

forbid.message: Uses a loop, not Math.Log or ToString

hints: `DigitCount`: start at 1 digit; while `n >= 10`, divide by 10 and add a digit.
